newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan options seen limited for beefing up stocks.
newsitem.headline: Japan options seen limited for beefing up stocks.

text.p: Japanese authorities appear content for now to let Tokyo's battered stock market find its own fair value -- and analysts say that quick fixes for the share slump are in short supply anyway.

The Tokyo stock market's main barometer, the 225-share Nikkei average, lost more than 2,000 points last week alone on spreading gloom over the government's ability to keep Japan's economic recovery on track and fulfil promises of vital reforms.

On Monday, the Nikkei bounced back, closing up 815.14 points, or 4.71 percent, at 18.118.79. Brokers said, however, the rise was mostly technical and that the market still lacked confidence in the government and in the economy.
In the past, drastic share price falls have prompted authorities to save the day with such steps as share purchases by public funds, big spending packages or interest rate cuts.
Officials have signalled, however, that they have no intention of repeating past practice -- at least for now.
On Monday, a Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) executive urged the ruling party's policy chief to study steps to deal with the share slide but ruled out a quick fix, Jiji news agency said.

Vice Trade Minister Tsutomu Makino, meanwhile, told a news conference that the trade ministry did not expect the weak share prices to hurt the economy and that his ministry was not mulling any steps to deal with the stock slump.
In part, the hands-off stance reflects a change of heart by policy makers who say they now believe that market forces should be left to operate without government interference.

"It's a shift from an underlying philosophy of big government to small government, from regulation to deregulation and from bailout to 'live and let die'," said Jesper Koll, chief economist at JP Morgan in Tokyo.
Politicians and bureaucrats have been lauding deregulation and market forces as the saviours of the nation's economic future, even as critics doubt their true intentions.
"They want to give the appearance that they have turned over a new leaf and are going to let market forces operate," said Ron Bevacqua, a senior economist at Merrill Lynch Japan.
Viable options for bailing out the stock market are at any rate limited, although analysts say authorities could be pressured to make an effort if the Nikkei approaches 15,000.
That is the level at which banks' unrealised profits on shareholdings would evaporate, eroding their ability to tackle their bad debts and pushing many into the red.
Interest rates are at rock-bottom levels and have been there since September 1995, when the Bank of Japan slashed its official discount rate to 0.5 percent to bolster the economy.

On the budgetary side, the government is touting the next business year from April 1 as the first year of a fiscal reconstruction aimed at getting Japan's huge budget deficit under control. "Anything they could do would require a major loss of face," a foreign strategist said.
Reneging on a commitment to raise the sales tax to five percent from three percent this year would be at best embarrassing and possibly politically disastrous, analysts said.

Some added, however, there was still scope to reverse a decision to eliminate two trillion yen ($17.2 billion) worth of special income tax cuts this year, while others suggested a cut in the securities transaction tax, which makes Tokyo an expensive place to trade shares.
Rescuing the market with a so-called "PKO" (price-keeping operation) using public pension funds would also go against the laissez-faire grain.
Such efforts have come under fire in the past for merely postponing the day of reckoning, and doubts also exist about how effective a "PKO" would be this time.

The government also argues that the market's outlook for the economy is too pessimistic, and is expected to reiterate its view that a gradual recovery is on course when its Economic Planning Agency issues a monthly report on Tuesday.
Many analysts, meanwhile, say that what the stock market really needs is some sign that Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto will follow reform rhetoric with substantive action soon.
Hashimoto in November pledged a five-year "Big Bang" programme to liberalise Japan's financial markets but details are still to be worked out.

"The debate is over the shape of things to come in the 21st century, but the illness is clear, so the remedy should be clear and speedy," said Yasunori Sone, a political scientist at Keio University. ($1=116 yen)
